ThingDef.label: Sudajii
ThingDef.description:
Sudajii (also called Itajii or Nagajii) is a tall evergreen tree that forms lucidophyll forest mainly in the warm-temperate regions of southern Honshu, Shikoku, and Kyushu.

Forests dominated by shii trees were already widespread in southwestern Japan by the Early Jomon period, and Early Jomon use of Castanopsis fruits has been confirmed at the Ireibaru site in Okinawa.

Its wood has been used for buildings and implements, tannin from the bark for dyeing items such as fishing nets, and its seeds as food.

ThingDef.label: Japanese beech
ThingDef.description:
Japanese beech (buna; also called Shirobuna or Honbuna; written 山毛欅, 橅, or 椈 in Japanese) is a large deciduous tree representative of Japan's cool-temperate zone, where it forms extensive mountain forests.

Cool-temperate forests containing Fagus are also known from northern Honshu in the Jomon period, and examples from the late Heian through medieval period show Fagus wood being selectively used for turned wooden objects such as lacquerware.

In modern Japan it is also used for furniture, interior materials, mushroom-growing logs, and firewood.

ThingDef.label: Shirabiso
ThingDef.description:
Shirabiso (written 白檜曽 in Japanese; also called Shirabe) is a tall evergreen conifer that forms climax forest in Honshu's subalpine zone.

On Mt. Ontake in the central mountains, subalpine conifer forests of Shirabiso, Veitch's silver fir, spruce, and related trees spread across the mountain slopes.

By the later medieval period, Ontake had become a destination for mountain asceticism and religious ascent, and forests such as these were part of a mountain-worship landscape distinct from settled lowlands.

ThingDef.label: Haimatsu
ThingDef.description:
Haimatsu (written 這松 in Japanese) is an evergreen dwarf pine distributed in alpine areas from Hokkaido to central and northern Honshu, where it forms dense creeping thickets above the treeline.

Its relict distribution is thought to reflect northern cold-climate plants that moved south during the glacial periods and remained at high elevations after the climate warmed.

Mt. Ontake became a destination for religious ascent from the later medieval period, and today Haimatsu scrub spreads across its alpine zone.
